A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same decision-theoretic framework and retain the one-max search and contract-scheduling applications. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic evaluations of contract scheduling and one-max search, plus experiments on four currency series, in Section 5 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on ski rental, one-max search, and contract scheduling, including currency and Bitcoin data, in Section 6 and Appendices C.4 and D.

M1.justification: v2 introduces ski-rental adaptations that select buying thresholds through critical-point optimization, average-distance minimization, and cost-based CVaR minimization (Section 3 and Appendix A, Algorithm 1). These add substantive decision procedures. The earlier one-max search and contract-scheduling methods are largely retained across renaming and relocation.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluation of ski rental, introducing a cost-minimization task absent from v1's experiments. Appendix D.3 also adds minute-level Bitcoin/USD data from 2020–2024. The original synthetic applications and four EUR exchange-rate series remain covered.

E2.justification: The new ski-rental experiments compare against three configurations of Benomar and Perchet's BP_rho algorithms. For one-max search, v1's cited PO and HA comparators correspond to v2's PO1 and delta-Tol, while PO2 is additionally evaluated in synthetic and real-data comparisons. Contract scheduling retains its two baseline methods.

E3.justification: The main synthetic one-max experiment changes from unbounded robustness and predictions uniform on [400,600] to r=100 and predictions uniform on [10,100], retaining M=1000. v2 replaces the percentage-of-time improvement metric with expected cost, profit, or completed-contract length alongside average ratios. It also revises predictive distributions and risk-parameter configurations.

E4.justification: v2 adds ski-rental sensitivity studies and tests robustness parameter r and prediction-sampling parameter z for both ski rental and one-max search. Earlier error-range, weight-function, and risk-parameter studies are revised and expanded in Appendices C.4 and D. Table 30 adds price-range analysis to explain differences across real-data series.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages without uncertainty intervals; v2 systematically adds 95% confidence intervals to synthetic and real-data results. Synthetic evaluations now report 1,000 repetitions rather than 100, while real-data evaluations retain 10,000 runs. The interval-construction procedure is not specified.

E6.justification: Numerical results are extensively replaced and expanded. For example, the one-max Max/Avg ratios of 9.26/10.51 in v1 Table 2 become 4.394/4.447 in v2 Table 2 under revised settings, so these are not same-setting gains. v2 also adds ski-rental and Bitcoin results, expected-return metrics, and revised currency outcomes and rankings.

T1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix A add ski-rental ideal-performance results, a critical-point optimization theorem, and a CVaR derivation with proofs. Appendix B supplies a proof for the previously stated one-max ideal-performance result. Most earlier one-max and contract-scheduling mathematics is retained in Appendices B and C, rather than newly introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions expand the claimed applications from two problems to three, adding optimization among ski-rental algorithms with incomparable performance functions. The core distance-based and risk-based framework remains, but the claimed constructive scope substantially increases.

C2.justification: v1 Appendix A.1 explains Gaussian weighting as increasing unweighted contract-scheduling ratios by emphasizing small errors; v2 Appendix C.4 instead presents concentrated Gaussian weights as beneficial. v2 also adds interpretations of robustness and sampling sensitivity, expected-return/risk tradeoffs, and Bitcoin's larger price variation, while retaining the qualification that real-data rankings depend on the series.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix D.3 adds a Bitcoin data-source reference and specifies its dates, minute-level frequency, and 2,630,880 observations. Conversely, the 0.001 discretization step for searching the contract-scheduling parameter, stated in v1 Section 5.1, is no longer documented. These are limited reproducibility-information changes.

R1.justification: Benomar and Perchet's work on incomparable Pareto-optimal algorithms becomes a central motivation and evaluated comparison. v2 substantially expands ski-rental and related rent-or-buy literature, including multi-shop, multi-option, and power-management connections, while removing several older contract-scheduling citations. The established ROC and CVaR connections remain.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: ski rental leads the applications, most one-max proofs move to Appendix B, and detailed contract scheduling moves to Appendix C. Experimental sections are extensively rewritten around baselines, datasets, evaluation, and discussion. The introduction, conclusion, prediction notation, and tolerance terminology also change throughout.

P2.justification: v1's experimental performance-curve Figures 2–9 are removed. v2 adds two ski-rental performance illustrations and redraws and relocates the game illustration as Figure 3. Compact grid tables become wide tables with grouped method columns, confidence-interval rows, and expected-return metrics, accompanied by numerous new parameter-comparison and real-data tables.

improvement.justification: v2 provides useful broader evaluation, expected-return measurements, and confidence intervals, but introduces a substantive defect in its new ski-rental theory. Theorem 3 omits the t*<T restriction used in its derivation: with b=T=10, alpha=0.9, and a uniform horizon on [0,40], Equation (7) gives 0.5 although the defined worst-tail cost is 20. The empirical additions therefore coexist with an unreliable central new guarantee, preventing a confident judgment of net overall improvement.
